course_description:
This course provides a current overview of cutting-edge innovation in biomanufacturing biotechnology. We will cover, in detail, specific enabling technologies driving change in biomanufacturing industries. This includes, but not limited to:

Students will learn about the current global trends in biomanufacturing and how cutting-edge biomanufacturing tools are changing industries to meet demand.

Course Description: This is a new course, offered for the first time in 2025. The course is designed to build on the basic information provided in courses such as BIOT7018 (Biologics) to explore how critical new pharmaceutically and industrially important biological molecules are manufactured on a large scale. This course provides a cutting-edge overview of innovation in global biomanufacturing. It explores how critical pharmaceutical and industrial biological molecules are manufactured at scale, with a strong emphasis on sustainable manufacturing platforms.

The curriculum is structured around four key modules:

Practical Component: Students will engage in a Pilot-Scale Beer Fermentation practical at the Andrew N. Liveris Building. This hands-on experience covers the entire biomanufacturing workflow, from mashing and boiling to fermentation and quality control, requiring students to perform mass and redox balances and evaluate product quality.

Additional timetable information
Lectures and Workshops:
The 2 hours of lectures per week are timetabled as a single 2-hour block. There is also a 2-hour workshop each week. Both sessions are highly interactive and involve active learning activities; therefore, attendance at both sessions is anticipated. Please note that while the lectures will be recorded, workshop sessions MAY NOT be recorded.
Pilot-Scale Beer Fermentation Practical:
Starting in Week 2, students will participate in a hands-on practical component delivered in a group-wise manner.
Group Structure:
Students will be divided into groups of ~15 participants.
Brewing Session:
Each group will carry out their primary practical work in a 3-hour block scheduled at the same time as the weekly workshop. This session includes a brewhouse instrumentation tour and the brewing process (mashing, boiling, and inoculation) in the Andrew N. Liveris (46) Level-1 Pilot Hall.
Analytical Session:
In the week following their brewing session, each group will attend a separate 1-hour session to perform specific analytical measurements (such as optical density and specific gravity) to monitor the progress of their fermentation.
Important Note:
Students must complete the assigned practical induction (in Week 1) before attending their scheduled session. Attendance is mandatory as information provided during these sessions is required for the individual Beer Fermentation Practical Report.
course_aims:
The course aims to enable students to:

a) Develop an understanding of the theoretical and practical aspects of large-scale protein expression systems and emerging biomanufacturing technologies.

b) Evaluate and identify scalable, sustainable, and future-ready biomanufacturing platforms capable of delivering real-world impact.

c) Apply principles of biomass valorisation and nanomaterials engineering to utilise waste streams as resources for environmental, food, and health applications.

d) Critically assess sustainable biomanufacturing approaches, including life cycle assessment, techno-economic analysis, regulatory considerations, and stakeholder engagement, and understand the upstream and downstream bioprocessing steps required for both traditional fermentation processes and advanced biologics manufacture.

e) Apply knowledge of current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP), regulatory frameworks, and analytical techniques used in the quality assurance and control of biomanufactured products.

learning_outcomes.description: Use their knowledge and expertise to evaluate biomanufacturing technologies and trouble shoot expression technologies.

Critically evaluate the environmental, economic, regulatory, and stakeholder considerations involved in new biomanufacturing processes, and synthesise these perspectives to inform evidence-based decision-making.

Critically assess the downstream processing requirements for large-scale biological manufacture, justifying the purpose, sequence, and trade-offs of each stage in the context of process efficiency and product quality.
Perform and analyse data generated using key analytical techniques critical in the evaluation of biomanufacturing products and procedures.
Interpret and apply current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP) requirements in biomanufacturing, and critically evaluate complex scenarios and case studies for regulatory compliance and risk.

Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
You are required to submit assessable items on time. If you fail to meet the submission deadline for any assessment item, then 10% of the maximum possible mark for the assessment item (assessment ‘marked from’ value) will be deducted as a late penalty for every day (or part day) late after the due date. For example, if you submit your assignment 1 hour late, you will be penalised 10%; if your assignment is 24.5 hours late, you will be penalised 20% (because it is late by one 24-hour period plus part of another 24-hour period). 10% will be deducted per day for up to 7 calendar days, at which point your submission will receive a mark of zero (0) unless an extension has been approved.
In most instances one or more hurdles will apply to your assessment item so you will need to submit it to fulfil the requirements of the course regardless of how late it is and the mark you are likely to be awarded.
